title: Fractions are slices, and true or false
summary: Cut fractions into the same size slices, then puzzle out who is a knight and who is a knave.

problems.prompt: What is 96 x 104?
explanation: Both numbers sit an equal distance from 100, one below and one above, so this is (100-4)(100+4), a difference of squares.
That always equals 100 squared minus 4 squared: 10000 - 16 is 9984.
problems.useAgain: when two numbers sit the same distance above and below a round number, since (100-n)(100+n) is always 100 squared minus n squared.
hints: Both numbers are the same distance from 100, just on opposite sides.
(100-4)(100+4) is always 100 squared minus 4 squared, try that instead of long multiplication.
problems.socraticHint: If you multiplied 96 by 104 with long multiplication and got a different answer, which step would you check first: the squaring of 100, or the squaring of 4?

variant.prompt: What is 94 x 106?

problems.prompt: What is 1000 minus 387?
explanation: Round 387 up to 400, since that is an easier number to subtract.
You subtracted 13 too many, so add 13 back: 600 + 13 is 613.
problems.useAgain: when subtracting a number that is close to a round number.
hints: Round 387 up to the nearest hundred first.
You will need to add back the amount you rounded up by.
problems.socraticHint: Instead of rounding down, what if you counted up from 387 to 1000 in friendly jumps? How many jumps would it take, and how big would the last one be?

variant.prompt: What is 1000 minus 489?

problems.prompt: What is 48 divided by 6, plus 7?
explanation: Do the inside part first, then the rest. Here the inside part is the division.
48 divided by 6 is 8.
8 plus 7 is 15.
problems.useAgain: when a problem has two steps, divide first and then add.
hints: Do the division before the addition.
48 divided by 6 is a whole number.
problems.socraticHint: If you added 7 to 48 before dividing by 6, would you still be answering the same question? What does that tell you about why the order matters here?

variant.prompt: What is 54 divided by 6, plus 8?

problems.prompt: What is 15% of 200?
explanation: 5% of 200 is half of that, which is 10.
15% is 10% plus 5%, so 20 plus 10 is 30.
problems.useAgain: when a percent breaks nicely into a 10% piece and a 5% piece.
hints: Find 10% first, it is just one tenth.
5% is half of 10%. Add the two pieces together.
problems.socraticHint: Could you think of 15% as three equal five-percent pieces instead of two pieces added together? What would each piece be worth?

variant.prompt: What is 15% of 160?

problems.prompt: What is 7 x 8 x 5?
explanation: Multiply 8 x 5 first, since that gives a round number: 40.
Now multiply 7 x 40, which is 280.
problems.useAgain: when three numbers multiply together, pick two that make a round number first.
hints: Look for two of the three numbers that multiply to a round number.
8 and 5 make a nice round number together.
problems.socraticHint: Does it matter which two of the three numbers you multiply first, or would you land on the same total no matter which pair you pick?

variant.prompt: What is 6 x 9 x 5?

problems.prompt: What is 37 x 44 minus 37 x 34?
explanation: Share the factor: both products use the same number, 37, so pull it out front instead of multiplying twice: 37 x (44 - 34).
44 minus 34 is 10, and 37 x 10 is 370.
This trick, share the factor, turns two multiplications into one subtraction and one easy multiplication.
problems.useAgain: when two multiplications share the same number, since pulling it out front turns the problem into one easy subtraction.
hints: Both products use the same number, 37. Try pulling it out front instead of multiplying twice.
37 x (44 - 34) is the same total, but the subtraction inside is easy.
problems.socraticHint: If 37 is multiplied in one place and subtracted after being multiplied in another, does it matter what 37 is, or only what is left after you combine the other two numbers?

variant.prompt: What is 58 x 23 minus 58 x 13?

problems.prompt: What is half of 3/4, as a fraction?
explanation: 3/4 is 3 quarter-slices.
Cut each of those 3 quarter-slices in half. Now every slice is an eighth instead of a quarter.
There are still 3 slices, just smaller ones, so half of 3/4 is 3/8. That is why the bottom number doubles.
problems.useAgain: when you need half of a fraction and want to picture the slices getting smaller.
hints: Multiplying by 1/2 means the bottom number doubles.
The top number stays where it is, only the bottom changes.
problems.socraticHint: If you folded a strip of paper shaded three quarters in half, how many total pieces would the whole strip be cut into now?

variant.prompt: What is half of 5/6, as a fraction?

problems.prompt: A ticket costs $19.99. Using a mental shortcut, what is the total cost of 3 tickets?
explanation: $19.99 is one cent less than $20, so round it up to $20 first: 3 x 20 is $60.
You added 1 cent extra three times, 3 cents too many, so subtract them back: $60 minus $0.03 is $59.97.
problems.useAgain: when a price sits just a cent or two below a round dollar amount and you are adding several of them.
hints: 19.99 is only a cent away from a much rounder number.
Round up to 20, multiply by 3, then take back the extra cents you added.
problems.socraticHint: If you added three copies of 20 instead of three copies of 19.99, how many extra cents did you sneak in, and what do you owe back at the end?

variant.prompt: A ticket costs $9.98. Using a mental shortcut, what is the total cost of 4 tickets?

explanationFigure.alt: The cross net folding into a cube: drag to turn it, slide to fold it, and watch which squares meet.

problem.prompt: Which of these flat shapes folds up into a closed cube, with no gaps and no squares left over?

figure.alt: Four flat shapes to compare, labeled A to D. Shape A: a straight strip of six squares in a single row. Shape B: a cross shape, a column of four squares stacked top to bottom, with one extra square on the left of the second square from the top, and one extra square on the right of that same square, six squares in total. Shape C: a rectangle of six squares, arranged two rows of three. Shape D: a cross shape like a plus sign, a column of four squares, with one extra square on the left of the second square from the top, one extra square on the right of that same square, and one more square attached below the bottom square, seven squares in total.

explanation: Fold it in your head, one square at a time. Start with the middle square of the cross and keep it flat: that becomes the front face.
Fold the square to its left back a quarter turn to become the left face. Fold the square to its right back a quarter turn to become the right face.
Fold the square above the middle back a quarter turn to become the top face. Fold the square below it back a quarter turn to become the bottom face.
The last square is attached to that bottom square. Swing it back one more quarter turn and it lands directly opposite the front, as the back face.
Six squares, six different faces, nothing overlaps: the cross folds into a closed cube.
The straight strip and the rectangle both make two squares land on the same face when you fold them this way. The seven-square shape has one square too many to begin with.
problem.useAgain: when you need to check whether a flat shape folds up into a closed box.
hints: Count the squares in each shape first. A cube needs exactly six faces.
Try folding each shape in your head, one square at a time, and watch for two squares landing in the same spot.
problem.socraticHint: When a cube is folded closed, the front and back faces always end up directly opposite each other. In each shape, can you spot which square would land across from which?

variant.prompt: Four flat shapes, labeled A to D. Shape A: a rectangle of six squares, arranged two rows of three. Shape B: a straight strip of six squares in a single row. Shape C: a cross shape, a column of four squares stacked top to bottom, with one extra square on the left of the second square from the top, and one extra square on the right of that same square, six squares in total. Shape D: a cross shape like a plus sign, a column of four squares, with one extra square on the left of the second square from the top, one extra square on the right of that same square, and one more square attached below the bottom square, seven squares in total. Which of these flat shapes folds up into a closed cube, with no gaps and no squares left over? Sketch each shape on graph paper before you choose.

problems.prompt: Three of these fractions are all the same amount. Which one does not belong?
explanation: Cut every fraction into the same size slices to compare them: 6/10, 9/15 and 3/5 all shrink down to the same fraction.
6/10 divided by 2 is 3/5. 9/15 divided by 3 is also 3/5. So those two match 3/5 exactly.
5/8 does not shrink down to 3/5 no matter what you divide by, so it is the odd one out.
problems.useAgain: when you need to spot which fraction in a group is not equivalent to the others.
hints: Try shrinking each fraction down to its simplest form and compare.
Two of the fractions shrink down to exactly the same simplest fraction; only one does not.
problems.socraticHint: If you shrank all four fractions down to their simplest form, three of them would land on the exact same fraction. Which one would be left standing alone?

variant.prompt: Three of these fractions are all the same amount. Which one does not belong?

problems.prompt: Which of these fractions is NOT equivalent to 5/8?
explanation: Same slice: each option should equal 5/8 when both top and bottom are scaled by the same whole number.
15/24 is 5/8 x 3, 20/32 is 5/8 x 4, and 35/56 is 5/8 x 7, so those three match exactly.
25/39 would need a bottom of 40 to match 5/8 scaled by 5, not 39, so it is the one that does not belong.
problems.useAgain: when you need to check whether several fractions are truly equivalent to a given fraction, not just close to it.
hints: Try scaling 5/8 by 3, 4, 5 and 7 and compare each result to the options.
One option changes its top number correctly but not its bottom number to match.
problems.socraticHint: If a fraction is truly equivalent to 5/8, what must be true about both its top and its bottom at the same time?

variant.prompt: Which of these fractions is NOT equivalent to 3/7?

explanationFigure.alt: A 6 by 6 grid of 36 squares, with 6 squares shaded, showing that the red squares are 6 out of 36, which shrinks to 1 out of 6.

problems.prompt: A grid has 36 equal squares. Half of them are shaded blue, and of the squares that are NOT shaded blue, one third are shaded red. What fraction of the whole grid is shaded red, in lowest terms?
explanation: Half of 36 squares are shaded blue, so 18 squares are blue and 18 are not.
Red is one third of the non-blue squares: one third of 18 is 6.
6 red squares out of 36 total is 6/36, which shrinks to 1/6.
problems.useAgain: when a shaded amount is described as a fraction of a fraction, and you need the reduced fraction of the whole.
hints: Work out how many squares are not blue before you find the red ones.
Red is one third of the non-blue group, not one third of the whole grid.
problems.socraticHint: Is one third of the non-blue squares the same amount as one third of the whole grid, or something smaller?

variant.prompt: A grid has 40 equal squares. Two fifths of them are shaded green, and of the squares that are NOT shaded green, one quarter are shaded yellow. What fraction of the whole grid is shaded yellow, in lowest terms?

problems.prompt:
Deshawn reduced 36/48 to lowest terms like this:
Line 1: 36 and 48 are both divisible by 4.
Line 2: 36 divided by 4 is 9.
Line 3: 48 divided by 4 is 12.
Line 4: So 36/48 in lowest terms is 9/12.
Which line is wrong?
explanation: Line 4 is wrong: 9/12 is not yet in lowest terms, since 9 and 12 still share a factor of 3.
Lines 1 through 3 are all correct: 36 and 48 do share a factor of 4. Dividing each by 4 really does give 9 and 12.
Same slice means shrinking all the way to the smallest possible slice size, so once you reach 9/12, check for a leftover common factor.
Divide 9 and 12 by 3: 9 divided by 3 is 3, and 12 divided by 3 is 4. So 36/48 in lowest terms is really 3/4.
problems.useAgain: when you reduce a fraction and want to check whether it has truly reached its simplest form.
hints: Every line's division is done correctly, so look past the arithmetic and ask what counts as 'lowest terms.'
After dividing by one common factor, check whether the two new numbers still share another factor bigger than 1.
problems.socraticHint: If two numbers can both be divided by 4, could they still share another common factor after that, like 2 or 3?

variant.prompt:
Marisol reduced 28/42 to lowest terms like this:
Line 1: 28 and 42 are both divisible by 7.
Line 2: 28 divided by 7 is 4.
Line 3: 42 divided by 7 is 6.
Line 4: So 28/42 in lowest terms is 4/6.
Which line is wrong?

explanationFigure.alt: A 5 by 5 grid of the badge's 25 lights, with 15 lit, showing that the diamond's 3 out of 5 is the same amount as 15 out of 25.

problems.prompt: Your badge lights up different amounts of its 25 LEDs for three icons: the heart lights 9/25 of the grid, the diamond lights 3/5 of the grid, and the star lights 11/25 of the grid. Put the icons in order from fewest LEDs lit to most.
explanation: Cut all three into the same size slices using 25ths: the diamond's 3/5 becomes 15/25, since 5 times 5 is 25.
Now compare 9/25, 11/25 and 15/25 directly, since they all have the same bottom number.
9 is the smallest, then 11, then 15, so the order from fewest LEDs to most is heart, star, diamond.
problems.useAgain: when you need to put fractions with different bottoms in order from smallest to largest.
hints: Give every fraction the same bottom number of 25 before you compare them.
5 times 5 is 25, so multiply both parts of the diamond's fraction by 5.
problems.socraticHint: The diamond's fraction already looks simpler than the other two. What happens if you write it with a bottom of 25 like the others, instead of leaving it as fifths?

variant.prompt: Your badge lights up different amounts of its 25 LEDs for three shapes: the square lights 7/25 of the grid, the circle lights 2/5 of the grid, and the triangle lights 13/25 of the grid. Put the shapes in order from fewest LEDs lit to most.

problems.prompt: A number line from 0 to 1 is marked in eighths. Which mark is closest to 2/3?
explanation: Cut 2/3 and the eighths marks into the same size slices using 24ths: 2/3 is 16/24.
5/8 is 15/24 and 6/8 is 18/24. 16/24 is only 1 away from 15/24, but 2 away from 18/24.
So 5/8 is the closest mark to 2/3.
problems.useAgain: when you need to find which mark on a number line a fraction is closest to.
hints: Give 2/3 and the eighths the same bottom number so you can compare them directly.
24ths work for both thirds and eighths.
problems.socraticHint: Before doing exact math, if you pictured 2/3 on a rough number line marked in eighths, which mark would your eye land on first?

variant.prompt: A number line from 0 to 1 is marked in eighths. Which mark is closest to 1/3?

explanationFigure.alt: A 4 by 6 grid of the badge's 24 lights, with 7 shaded, showing that 7 out of 24 of the badge stays dark.

problems.prompt: Your badge has a 24-LED grid. The heart icon lights 5/12 of the grid. Your own drawn picture lights half of the LEDs that the heart does NOT light. What fraction of the whole grid is still dark, in lowest terms?
explanation: The heart lights 5/12 of the grid, leaving 7/12 not lit by the heart.
Your own picture lights half of that leftover 7/12, which is 7/24.
Add the two lit amounts on a common bottom of 24: 5/12 is 10/24, plus 7/24 is 17/24 lit in total.
Dark is whatever is left from the whole: 24/24 minus 17/24 is 7/24.
problems.useAgain: when a fraction of an already-leftover amount needs a common bottom before you can find what remains dark.
hints: Find the fraction NOT lit by the heart before you find what your own picture lights.
Add the two lit fractions on a common bottom before subtracting from the whole.
problems.socraticHint: Is half of the leftover LEDs the same fraction of the WHOLE grid as half of the grid itself?

variant.prompt: Your badge has a 20-LED grid. The diamond icon lights 3/10 of the grid. Your own drawn picture lights half of the LEDs that the diamond does NOT light. What fraction of the whole grid is still dark, in lowest terms?

problems.prompt: Knights always tell the truth, and knaves always lie. A says: '2 + 2 = 5.' What is A?
explanation: Every sentence is true or false, pick one. There is no third option.
'2 + 2 = 5' is a false sentence, since 2 + 2 is really 4.
A knight only ever says true things, so anyone who says a false sentence must be a knave.
problems.useAgain: when someone makes a claim and you need to know if they always tell the truth or always lie.
hints: Check whether the sentence A said is actually true or false in the real world.
One type of person always says something true, and the other type always says something false.
problems.socraticHint: Would someone who is completely incapable of lying ever feel comfortable saying a sentence that is actually false out loud?

variant.prompt: Knights always tell the truth, and knaves always lie. E says: '10 is an even number.' What is E?

problems.prompt: Knights always tell the truth, and knaves always lie. F says: '5 x 5 = 25.' What is F?
explanation: '5 x 5 = 25' is a true sentence.
A knave can only say false things, so anyone who says a true sentence must be a knight.
problems.useAgain: when a statement can be checked as simply true or false in the real world.
hints: Check whether F's sentence is actually true.
A knave could never say something true.
problems.socraticHint: If a person can only ever tell lies, what would have to be true about literally every sentence that comes out of their mouth?

variant.prompt: Knights always tell the truth, and knaves always lie. K says: 'A week has ten days.' What is K?

problems.prompt: Knights always tell the truth, and knaves always lie. C says: 'If I am a knight, then D is a knave.' What are C and D?
explanation: If then means: if this, then that. Check the if first.
If C is a knight, then C's statement is true.
Since the if part is true, the then part must also be true: D is a knave.
If C is a knave, then C's statement must be false. But the if part, 'C is a knight', would then be false.
That makes the whole if-then sentence automatically true, and a knave can never say something true. So C cannot be a knave.
That leaves only one option: C is a knight and D is a knave.
problems.useAgain: when a statement has the shape if this then that, and you need to check both cases.
hints: Try assuming C is a knave first and see if that causes a problem.
An if-then sentence with a false if part is automatically true, no matter what the then part says.
problems.socraticHint: What if you started by assuming C is a knight instead? Does C's sentence being true then pin down something specific about D?

variant.prompt: Knights always tell the truth, and knaves always lie. G says: 'If I am a knight, then H is a knight.' What are G and H?

problems.prompt: Knights always tell the truth, and knaves always lie. P says: 'Q is a knave.' Q says: 'P and I are different types.' What are P and Q?
explanation: Try P as a knight first. Then P's statement is true, so Q is a knave.
But if Q is a knave, Q's statement 'P and I are different types' must be false.
That means P and Q are actually the same type. P knight and Q knave are different types, so this breaks. P cannot be a knight.
So P is a knave. P's statement 'Q is a knave' is then false, so Q is a knight.
Q is a knight, so Q's statement is true: P and Q really are different types. P knave, Q knight are different types, so everything checks out.
problems.useAgain: when two people's statements refer to each other and you need to test both cases.
hints: Try each option for P and see if it leads to a contradiction.
When one person's lie or truth affects the other person's type, work through it one step at a time.
problems.socraticHint: Once you have picked a type for P, does Q's statement about being 'different' end up agreeing with itself, or contradicting itself?

variant.prompt: Knights always tell the truth, and knaves always lie. S says: 'T is a knave.' T says: 'S and I are different types.' What are S and T?

problems.prompt: True or false: a knight can make a statement that turns out to be false.
explanation: A knight always tells the truth, every single time.
That means a knight's statement can never turn out to be false, so this is false.
problems.useAgain: when you need to check whether a rule like always or never actually allows an exception.
hints: Think about what 'always tells the truth' really means.
If something always happens, can the opposite ever happen too?
problems.socraticHint: Is a knight like a person who tells the truth almost all the time, or does 'always' promise something stronger than that?

variant.prompt: True or false: a knight can accidentally tell a lie.

problems.prompt: True or false: a knave can make a statement that turns out to be true.
explanation: A knave always lies, every single time.
That means a knave's statement can never turn out to be true, so this is false.
problems.useAgain: when a rule says always and you need to test whether it has exceptions.
hints: Think about what 'always lies' really means.
If someone always lies, could one of their sentences slip through as true?
problems.socraticHint: If a knave tried to sneak in one true sentence just this once, would that break the very rule that makes them a knave?

variant.prompt: True or false: a knave can accidentally tell the truth.

problems.prompt: Explain why a person can never say 'I am a knave', whether that person is a knight or a knave.

mustMention: knave would be telling the truth

explanation: If this person were a knight, they only say true things, but 'I am a knave' would be false.
So a knight would be lying, which a knight can never do.
If this person were a knave, they only say false things, but 'I am a knave' would be true.
So a knave would be telling the truth, which a knave can never do.
Both cases break the rules, so no one, knight or knave, can ever say 'I am a knave'.
problems.useAgain: when a statement talks about itself and you need to check both cases before trusting it.
hints: Try assuming the person is a knight first, and see what goes wrong.
Then try assuming the person is a knave, and see what goes wrong there too.
problems.socraticHint: What makes this sentence different from an ordinary claim about someone else, and why might that difference trap both a knight and a knave?

steps.title: Explain it
steps.prompt: Pick the hardest knights-and-knaves problem. Write why your answer must be right, one idea per sentence. Name the idea you used.

steps.title: Explain back
steps.prompt: Say out loud how you solved it, as if to a friend.

extras.title: How your brain keeps this
extras.body:
Before the season starts, ten minutes on how your own brain keeps things. Everything in this app is built on it.

1. Reading something again feels like learning. It mostly is not. Pulling it back out of your head, without looking, is what makes it stay. That is why the mistake box brings a problem back weeks later in a new shape.
2. The gap matters. A thing you meet in week 3 and again in week 7 sticks far better than a thing you meet twice in one afternoon. The warm-ups do this on purpose.
3. Sleep is when the day's learning gets filed. A hard bar practised before bed is easier in the morning for a reason.
4. A mistake is data, not a mark against you. Finding out you were sure and wrong is the most useful moment of the week. That is why the app asks what made it feel certain.
5. Small and often beats long and rare. Four sittings of fifteen minutes teach more than one hour, in music and in math alike.

Now write one goal for this season in your own words in this week's Maker's Log. Make it something you will be able to do in week 12 that you cannot do today. At the last Showcase you read it back.

What to notice: which of the five you already do without being told, and which one you have been avoiding.
